text: What if I told you that right now, you are paying for things that quietly stopped being
worth it?
Not luxuries.
Normal.
Everyday purchases that felt smart a few years ago.
And the number 12 on this list is the one almost nobody ever checks.
Prices keep climbing.
Wages for many people do not keep up.
So can I afford it?
Is no longer the right question.
The better one is, is this still worth it?
Let's go through 12 things that fail that test in 2027.
We start with the one in your pocket.
Number one.
Food delivery apps.
The cost arrives in small pieces.
A delivery fee, a service fee, a tip.
And behind the scenes, restaurants often pay these platforms 15-30% per order.
So many raise their menu prices on the app.
A meal that costs 12 in the restaurant can reach 20 by the time it hits your door.
Do that twice a week and you're paying hundreds extra a year just to skip a short drive.
Delivery was meant for tired days.
For many people it became the default.
And the default is the most expensive habit there is.
But the next one costs far more.
Number two.
Brand new cars.
A new car loses roughly a fifth of its value in the first year and often close to half
within five.
At a big loan and you can owe more than the car is worth for years.
Smart buyers let someone else take that first loss.
A car a few years old has already survived the steepest drop and still has years
of reliable driving left.
You get most of the car for a fraction of the cost.
A new car is not wrong.
It is just one of the most expensive ways to get from A to B.
And the next one is a payment that rarely even gets used.
Number three.
Gym memberships you don't use.
Forty a month is 480 a year.
If you go twice a month every visit costs you 20.
At that price you could pay per class and still come out ahead.
Gyms know this.
Their model depends on many members paying and few showing up.
Walking, body weight workouts, free videos, a local park, they all cost nothing.
A membership is only worth it if your feet actually go through the door.
And speaking of paying for a peace of mind, here is number four.
Number four.
Extended warranties.
At the checkout, they ask if you want to protect your purchase.
It sounds responsible.
It is also one of the most profitable things a store sells
because most products never break during that period.
Many items already come with a basic warranty.
Many credit cards add more.
A smarter move is keeping that money in your own small emergency fund.
Something breaks, you cover it.
If nothing breaks, which is far more likely, the money is still yours.
Number five.
Cheap, fast fashion.
A shirt for the price of a sandwich feels like a win.
But the right way to measure clothes is cost per wear.
A $15 shirt that dies after five wears costs three each time.
A $60 shirt that lasts 60 wears costs one.
The cheap one was the expensive one all along.
Fewer, better basics usually cost less over time.
Now, something almost everyone is holding right now.
Number six.
Upgrading your phone every year.
Phones used to improve in huge leaps.
Today, the gap between one generation and the next
is often small, but the price is not.
And when you sell the old one,
you get back only a part of what you paid.
So the real cost of upgrading
is the money you lose again and again.
Ask one honest question.
What can the new phone do that mine cannot
in a way I would actually notice?
If you struggle to answer, you have your answer.
And speaking of paying extra for a name,
number seven is in your kitchen.
Number seven.
Name brands for everyday basics
walk down any supermarket aisle.
Two products sit side by side.
One has the famous name.
The other is planer and cheaper.
A store brand pain reliever contains
the same active ingredient
and the same strength as the famous one.
With food and cleaning products,
the store version is often close to identical
at a price 20 to 30% lower.
The extra cost goes mostly to advertising.
Try the store brand on five items this month.
If you cannot taste the difference,
you just found money that was never needed.
Number eight.
The daily coffee shop drink, let's be fair.
A coffee shop is a break,
a ritual, a place to sit.
That has real value.
But one $5 drink every workday
adds up to around 1300 a year,
while coffee at home costs a small fraction of that.
You do not have to give it up.
Make it twice a week, a treat instead of a routine.
A habit you chose is a pleasure.
A habit you never questioned is a leak
and there is one purchase type
that makes leaks much worse.
Number nine.
Buy now, pay later.
Split it into four easy payments.
It sounds like a friendly favor,
but it changes how your brain sees the price.
Studies suggest many people spend more
when they can split the cost.
And a noticeable share of users miss payments,
which brings fees and stress.
These small plans pile up
until your income is promised
to things you have already forgotten.
Here's a simple rule.
If you cannot afford it today,
ask why you want it today.
If you still want it in a few weeks, save for it.
If the desire fades,
you just kept your money without even trying.
The next one bleeds you slowly and legally.
Number 10.
Bank fees, a monthly account fee, an overdraft fee,
an ATM fee, a fee for dropping just below a minimum balance.
Each one is small.
Together, they can reach a surprising amount
and they buy you nothing.
Fee-free accounts exist.
You can ask your bank to remove a fee or simply switch.
Check your last three statements.
If you find a fee,
you just found the easiest money you will ever save.
Two left and they are connected.
Number 11.
Stacking streaming services.
Streaming started as a way to save money.
Then came more services,
each with its own exclusive shows and rising prices.
Four services at around 12 each is nearly 600 a year
and most people actively watch only one or two.
Try rotating, subscribe to one service,
watch what you want, cancel, then move to the next.
Shows do not disappear.
They wait for you.
Now, the one I promised.
The one almost nobody checks.
Number 12.
Subscriptions you forgot you had.
Think for a moment.
How many subscriptions are you paying for right now?
Apps, boxes, storage, trial plans
that quietly turned into paid ones.
Surveys often find that people underestimate
their subscription spending and forget some even exist.
That is no accident.
Companies make signing up easy and cancelling hard
and they count on you never looking.
So today, open your statement,
go back three months and mark every repeating charge.
For each one, ask three questions.
Did I use this in the last month?
Would I buy it again today?
Could I live without it?
If any answers no, cancel it.
A hundred a month,
invested for 20 years at a steady average return
could grow to around 50,000.
Not guaranteed, but that is how time works.
Look at what all 12 share.
Convenience, comfort, status, fear of missing out.
Each one makes spending feel normal,
even smart, until you do the math.
You do not need to cut them all.
If something truly brings you joy,
that is a good reason to spend.
The goal is simple.
Every purchase should be a choice you made,
not a habit that made you.
Because in 2027, the real skill is not earning more
or spending less, it is noticing.
And asking one question every time,
is this still worth it?
This video is for education and general information,
not personal financial advice.
Pick one thing from this list
and change it this week, just one.
And if this changed how you see your money,
watch the next video,
because there is one more spending trap
almost everyone falls into,
and it has nothing to do with shopping.
Prachodacha!
